speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) in respect of the collision at Joo Koon station on 15 November 2017, what were the control options available to the driver of the second train to stop the train before it collided into the rear of the first train; and (b) what are the usual control options available to drivers of trains on North-South and East-West Lines for manual or emergency braking.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: asked the Minister for Transport (a) before the collision at Joo Koon station on 15 November 2017, whether the operations control centre and the driver of the second train were aware that the protective bubbles of the first train had malfunctioned; (b) if so, whether there were other options that could have been taken to ensure that the second train remained stationary; and (c) whether there was any previous occasion when a train had continued to operate when its protective bubbles had malfunctioned.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As a result, the first train at Joo Koon station was operating without a protective bubble that ensures safe distances between trains.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Subsequent tests and re-enactments confirmed that the failure conditions must occur in a specific sequence for the protective bubble to be deactivated.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Thales, the supplier of the system, had not anticipated such a scenario.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: This was an isolated case with no precedent, even for Thales.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The Operations Control Centre (OCC) staff and the train captains did not know that the protective bubble could be deactivated.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: All North-South and East-West Line trains, including those involved in the collision at Joo Koon station, are equipped with an emergency stop button for the train captain to apply the brakes manually.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Based on train logs, the train captain in the second train was unable to engage these emergency brakes in time to avert a collision.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In addition, Thales is setting up a simulation facility, a simulator, in Singapore to strengthen the testing process.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The facility will enable the Land Transport Authority (LTA) and SMRT Corp to perform additional simulation tests in a controlled setting which is tailored to our local environment and the infrastructural conditions of our rail network before deploying on our train services.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The separation will continue until the rest of the East-West Line has fully transitioned to the new signalling system.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Meanwhile, we are speeding up the re-signalling project, and the extended engineering hours on the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) early closures and late openings will enable us to complete this transition by the middle of this year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, I understand from media reports and correct me if I am wrong here, that because of the failure conditions, the bubbles did not take place.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think there was a fixed distance of about 36 metres between the first and second trains.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I just heard from the Minister that the driver apparently applied the emergency brakes, or did he apply the brakes and they did not work?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, can I just clarify with the Minister on this point, whether or not the driver applied the emergency brakes or the automatic brakes to be used in emergency circumstances like what is available on the East-West and North-South Lines?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that is the case, subject to the Minister's answer, will LTA look into the condition of why the brakes did not come into effect, despite there being a braking distance of 36 metres?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question is, in light of what has just happened, which I agree could be quite unique, but nevertheless, for safety purposes, will SMRT be required to review its standard operating procedures (SOPs) in contingency situations like what we saw at Joo Koon, so that the OCC or the driver will be alerted to and will be required to apply the brakes when trains start to move in unforeseeable circumstances in order to prevent collisions from happening?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As I had explained, this situation was never anticipated by Thales themselves.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I did engineering but that was many years ago.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: One of my favourite subjects was computer programming.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Of course, many things have happened during the last 40-odd years.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Computer languages have improved and there are many more new languages and more efficiency tools.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But the basic principle of writing computer programme, I think, has not changed.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Which is, you start off by anticipating "what ifs".

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: All kinds of possible scenarios and therefore, you compose logic, diagrams and decision trees, before you start coding and converting each of the steps into a program, so that the computer knows what to do.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: A good computer programmer is one who has robustly and comprehensively thought of all possibilities so that computers or the robot would know how to react.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Unfortunately, in this instance, Thales had not anticipated such a possibility and, therefore, the assumption, both by Thales and the operator – the operators were trained by Thales – was that the deactivating of the bubble could not have happened.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Had we known, as I had explained in my answer, the driver would have converted it into manual mode, instead of leaving the train to be run by the computer.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: If it was in manual mode, there would have been an adequate reaction time.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: In hindsight, one can blame the captain, but I do not.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Because he was mentally not prepared and never trained to react under that kind of scenario.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: If I may just describe a little, though highly simplified, what kind of complications we have introduced prior to this incident.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: East-West Line is a complete line but we were doing the most complicated by requiring the signalling system to run on most part of the Line, on the old system, and then at some point, switch to a new system.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Therefore, the trains were being operated by two signalling systems – the old system and the new system.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: They were required to know when to do what.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: So, based on the location at the track, the new signalling system could be on "passive" mode or "active" mode.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: For the stretch of the East-West Line which is still on the old signalling system, the system is on passive mode.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: It is collecting and reporting information but not acting.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But after clearing a particular station, when it enters the Tuas West Extension, it switched into active mode.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: For the deactivation of the bubble to take place, several things must happen.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Unfortunately, on that day, all three things happened.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: First, the train must have developed some problem.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Trains carry a lot of computers and the computers' signalling equipment have to communicate with the track-side equipment of the new system.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: For that particular train that day, it was not able to communicate.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: When it is not able to communicate, the system, as a safety procedure, activate this bubble so that the trains would comply with the safety distances between trains.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: That was the first step and in this case, it happened.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Unfortunately, this was the sort of scenario that the programmer had not anticipated.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: When it was deactivated, well, the rest is history.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Now, the flaw has been rectified and corrected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I understand the explanation about the problem which is created by the software logic issue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: But my two questions today focused on the driver's access to the braking system of the train.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: This is important because whether it is a software logic issue that creates any situation or any other kind of glitch, software or otherwise, I would like to ask the Minister, whether in that accident or in ordinary circumstances, whether the train is operating on automatic mode or controlled manual mode, what is the access the driver or the OCC has to apply emergency braking, and what would be that expected reaction time?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Because the driver might have to switch from the automatic to manual mode, and from the manual mode, he could have activated the emergency button.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: On hindsight, it is easy to say, "Why did you not do this?" and "Why did you not do that?" A few months ago, I had a friend, a corporate lawyer, who called me frantically.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: As he approached a pedestrian crossing, he was quite clear that there was nobody.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: He slowed down but he did not stop.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: We do not normally stop in front of the pedestrian crossing unless we know that there is a pedestrian.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But the next second, he saw somebody on an e-scooter flung onto his windscreen.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: The rider must have been speeding right through.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But that was when my friend stopped, came down, assisted and called the ambulance.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: A few days later, he was informed by the hospital that the victim died.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: He knew he would be charged, he expected to be punished but he was very worried that he would be jailed.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: Being a lawyer, he checked up the law and asked me for advice.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I am not a lawyer; I cannot advise him much.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: But as a layman, I wonder: when you do not have sufficient reaction time, are you responsible?

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I asked him to get a lawyer and a proper forensic to see whether it could ascertain the speed of the e-scooter.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I think the Joo Koon situation is something like this, too.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think we move on to the next Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Alright, I will just allow the last question.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Just one clarification on what he just said.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I think it would depend on the design.

speaker: Mr Khaw Boon Wan
text: I am not perfectly sure of the answer, but I will check.
